Forgive my ignorance, but why compare taxes to GDP? Isn't GDP basically just how rich an area is? Maybe some of those top states have more rich people and natural resources than average, which doesn't really help us common folk decide what place is actually best. I would think a cost of living chart that includes taxes would be more useful.

It's basically a composite measure of their tax rate.

Let's say an area has no "income tax" but a high sales tax. Sales tax is an income tax (less what you don't spend on actuall goods). So if you spend only 20% of your income on physical goods in a store then that's 20% of your income taxed at an additional 8% (some areas).

So how do we merge income tax and sales tax when they are both income taxes? GDP is income, or at least taxes on someone in your state who is being taxed for their GDP activities shares a tax burden with you (divided proportionally by the elasticity of supply and demand).

Now if we didn't use tax/gdp and instead looked at tax per captia then we would essentially end up with what would be a GDP measurement that would be useless to us for tax purposes. West Virginia, who's tax rate is high would have a low tax per captia just because people don't have a lot of income to tax.

Basically a Tax per capita would always tell you to live in the country regardless of what the tax policy is.

Also GDP doesn't tell you how rich an area is. That would be GDP per capita.
